specPoints.text: Core practical 5: investigate the refractive index of glass, using a glass block

primer.text: Core practical 5 asks you to measure the refractive index of a glass block for yourself. You will trace a ray box beam through the block at several incidence angles, record the matching refraction angles and turn the pairs into a straight-line graph. Along the way you will name variables, choose sensible equipment and judge where errors creep in — the full experimental toolkit in one investigation.

lessons.title: Core Practical: Investigating Snell's law
lessons.opening: The apparatus is simple: a ray box, a protractor and a perspex block on paper. Trace the beam at one incidence angle after another, join the entry and exit points, and measure the refraction angle each time. Plotting the sine of one against the sine of the other gives a straight line, and the gradient of that line is the refractive index you set out to find.
keyPoints: The experiment investigates the refractive index of glass using a glass block.
The independent variable is the angle of incidence; the dependent variable is the angle of refraction.
Control variables include the same perspex block, the beam width and the light frequency.
Equipment: a ray box provides the beam, a protractor measures both angles, and plotting sin i against sin r gives a straight line whose gradient is the refractive index.
Systematic errors come from wrongly drawn perpendicular lines; random errors come from imprecise marking and the protractor resolution.

low.restatement: Shine the beam into the block at different angles, trace each path, measure both angles and read the refractive index off the gradient of the sine graph.
low.analogy: Fingerprinting glass: every material leaves its own straight-line signature when you plot sine against sine.
low.examPointer: Questions often ask only for the aim — "investigate the refractive index of glass using a glass block" — word it exactly.

medium.restatement: Changing the incidence angle while holding the block, beam and light fixed isolates how the refraction angle responds; the sine-sine plot linearises Snell's law so its gradient equals the index.
medium.analogy: A fair race: one runner varies, everything else — track, shoes, wind — stays identical, so the result means something.
medium.examPointer: Name all three variable roles in method questions; forgetting the control variables is the most common lost mark.

check.stem: In this investigation the angle of incidence is the:

options.text: control variable
options.explanation: The incidence angle is deliberately changed, not held constant.

options.text: dependent variable
options.explanation: The refraction angle is the measured outcome; the incidence angle is set first.

options.text: independent variable
options.explanation: The experimenter chooses each incidence angle, making it the independent variable.

options.text: resolution of the protractor
options.explanation: Resolution is an instrument property, not an experimental variable.

check.stem: A graph of sin i against sin r is plotted. The refractive index of the block is:

options.text: the gradient of the line
options.explanation: Snell's law makes sin i / sin r constant, so the straight line's gradient equals n.

options.text: the y-intercept
options.explanation: The line passes through the origin; the intercept carries no information.

options.text: the area under the line
options.explanation: Area has no meaning in this plot.

options.text: the number of data points
options.explanation: More points improve reliability, but never give the index.

check.stem: Which list gives control variables for this experiment?

options.text: the block used, the beam width and the light frequency
options.explanation: These are held constant so only the incidence angle changes.

options.text: the incidence angle, the refraction angle and the block used
options.explanation: The two angles are the variables being studied, not controls.

options.text: the protractor cost, the room colour and the time of day
options.explanation: These are irrelevant to the physics of refraction.

options.text: the beam width only
options.explanation: True but incomplete — the block and light frequency are controlled too.

check.stem: Which piece of equipment provides the narrow beam of light?

options.text: measure the angles to 1°
options.explanation: That is the protractor's job.

options.text: provide a narrow beam of light that refracts in the block
options.explanation: The ray box emits the narrow beam the experiment traces.

options.text: draw the outline of the block
options.explanation: The outline is drawn by pencil around the block.

options.text: plot the graph of sin i against sin r
options.explanation: Graphs are plotted afterwards from the results table.

check.stem: Drawing the 90° perpendicular lines incorrectly would introduce:

options.text: a random error reduced by repeating trials
options.explanation: A wrongly drawn line biases every reading the same way — that is systematic.

options.text: a systematic error; use a set square to draw them
options.explanation: The note names the misplaced perpendicular as a systematic error fixed with a set square.

options.text: no measurable effect on the results
options.explanation: Angles measured from a wrong normal are all shifted.

options.text: a safety hazard rather than an error
options.explanation: It affects accuracy, not safety.

check.stem: Name three items of equipment used in this investigation and give one purpose.
check.modelAnswer: Ray box (provides the narrow light beam), protractor (measures the incidence and refraction angles) and perspex block (refracts the beam) — any three items with a purpose.

check.stem: State one safety rule for this experiment and the reason behind it.
check.modelAnswer: Avoid looking directly into the ray box light, because the beam can damage the eyes.

check.stem: Explain why sin i is plotted against sin r rather than plotting the raw angles i against r.
check.modelAnswer: Snell's law keeps sin i / sin r constant at n, so the sine graph is a straight line through the origin whose gradient gives the refractive index, while plotting the raw angles would produce a curve that is hard to read a value from.

check.stem: One trial records an incidence angle of 30° and a refraction angle of 20°. Estimate the refractive index of the block and comment on the value.
check.modelAnswer: sin 30° / sin 20° = 0.500 / 0.342 = 1.46, which is about 1.5 — the expected refractive index for a perspex or glass block.

glossary.definition: The quantity deliberately changed by the experimenter; here, the angle of incidence.
The quantity measured as the outcome; here, the angle of refraction.
A quantity kept constant so it cannot skew the comparison.
The smallest change an instrument can reliably display, such as 1° on a protractor.
